query: For a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy initially in a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-containing state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its subsequent microstructural evolution and the associated retention or loss of corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance? The hypothesis should address the unresolved transformation pathway and kinetics while accounting for the tendency of these alloys to develop intermetallic compounds. Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the initial state, the relevant service-regime boundaries, supporting evidence from reported Mg-containing alloys, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: In a metastable single-phase lightweight Mg-containing high-entropy alloy (HEA), the first microstructural event on exposure to 300–500 °C in air is a Mg-driven, diffusion-controlled cellular decomposition that produces coherent, Mg-enriched L1₂-type nano-precipitates at f.c.c. matrix {100} planes.  As these precipitates grow and coarsen they locally deplete the surrounding matrix in Mg, which (1) removes the solid-solution strengthening contribution of Mg, (2) suppresses the original uniform protective Mg-rich surface oxide, and (3) provides galvanic micro-cells at the precipitate/matrix interface that accelerate corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.  If the precipitate volume fraction remains below ~8 vol % (achieved by quenching or service below ~300 °C), the matrix stays supersaturated, Mg remains available to form a continuous adherent MgAl₂O₄-rich surface scale, and the original corrosion/oxidation resistance is largely retained.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or solution-treated lightweight f.c.c. HEA (e.g., Al₁₀Mg₁₀Li₁₀Ti₂₀Cr₂₀Mn₂₀ wt %; exact composition immaterial) that is single-phase, chemically homogeneous and supersaturated in Mg (≈8–12 at %), showing high specific strength and a continuous Mg-rich surface oxide that affords good corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Isothermal exposure (aging) in laboratory air at 300–500 °C for 10⁻¹–10² h, followed by water-quench to preserve the evolved microstructure.
generation.conditions: Ambient pressure air; temperature window 300–500 °C (typical aerospace service range); no external mechanical load; samples with identical prior history except for thermal exposure time.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of coherent Mg-rich L1₂-structured nano-precipitates (≈3–20 nm) forming a semi-continuous network on {100} planes in the f.c.c. matrix.
generation.mechanism: 1. Positive chemical interaction parameter between Mg and the refractory sub-lattice drives uphill Mg diffusion (spinodal-like decomposition). 2. Coherent strain energy is minimized by forming plate-like L1₂ precipitates on {100} planes. 3. Local Mg depletion in the surrounding matrix reduces the activity of Mg at the surface, disrupting the original protective Mg-rich oxide film. 4. The resulting compositional gradients establish galvanic couples that accelerate localized corrosion and allow faster inward oxygen diffusion, so oxidation resistance deteriorates as precipitates coarsen.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unaged control, specimens aged ≥10 h at ≥400 °C will show: (a) TEM-visible 5–10 nm L1₂ precipitates enriched in Mg (≥40 at % Mg) on {100} planes; (b) a drop in open-circuit corrosion potential by ≥150 mV in 3.5 wt % NaCl; (c) at 700 °C oxidation, mass-gain rates at least 3× higher owing to non-protective, Mg-depleted, mixed oxides; (d) micro-probe maps revealing Mg depletion (≥30 % reduction vs. bulk) in 10–20 nm shells around the precipitates.
generation.baseline: Unaged, solution-treated material quenched to room temperature: single-phase f.c.c. solid solution with no detectable precipitates; continuous Mg-rich surface oxide; corrosion current density < 1 µA cm⁻² and parabolic oxidation constant kₚ ≈ 1×10⁻¹⁴ kg² m⁻⁴ s⁻¹ at 700 °C.
generation.boundary: Below 250 °C, Mg diffusivity is too low; no precipitates form within 100 h, so corrosion/oxidation resistance is retained.  Above ~550 °C, precipitates lose coherency and coarsen to >50 nm, leading to re-equilibration of Mg in the matrix and restoration of a thicker, but less adherent, MgO/Al₂O₃ composite scale; therefore the predicted deterioration peaks between 350 and 500 °C and declines at higher T or very long times.
generation.uncertainty: Lacking quantitative diffusion data for Mg in multi-principal element matrices, the exact critical time (≈10 h) and precipitate volume fraction (≈8 vol %) thresholds are estimates; the crystal structure could locally vary (possible D0₃ ordering) in very Mg-rich alloys, altering the coherency window.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically cast and solution-treated coupons.  Age one set at 400 °C for 25 h; keep the other as-solutionized.  Characterize both by: (i) high-resolution STEM-EDS for precipitate identification and Mg distribution; (ii) potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt % NaCl at 25 °C; (iii) isothermal oxidation at 700 °C for 10 h followed by mass-gain measurement and X-ray diffraction of the scale.
measurements: Precipitate size, number density, and composition by STEM-EDS
Matrix Mg content by APT or STEM-EDS line profiles
Open-circuit potential and corrosion current density
Oxidation mass-gain vs. time; calculated kₚ
Surface oxide phase assemblage by XRD / Raman
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following are true: (1) Aged samples show no Mg-rich nano-precipitates or no Mg depletion zones; (2) Corrosion potential differs by <50 mV and corrosion current by <20 % between aged and unaged samples; (3) Oxidation rate constants of aged samples are ≤1.5× that of unaged controls despite precipitate formation.
